activity.text: Reconnecting with an old friend this week sparked a Jean de La Fontaine vibe in me. The 🤗
activity.captured_text: Reconnecting with an old friend this week sparked a Jean de La Fontaine vibe in me. The 🤗 & the 🚜 Once upon a time, a little Hug and a little Tractor made a promise to each other : go discover the world, and meet again in seven years, at the exact same place, to see who had the most adventurous adventures. The little Hug decided to set sail on the vast ocean, although everyone told her there was nothing to find out there. She was convinced that somewhere existed a source — an open source — where creation itself could originate from. The little Tractor, on the contrary, decided to stay on firm ground. He wanted to stay in touch with concrete reality. But he was determined to drive so far that he would reach the top of the world, something no little Tractor had done before him. For years, the little Hug seemed lost in infinite waters, without a direction. But every day, fishes, small and large, joined her and swam along as she sailed. For years, the little Tractor climbed. Despite early engine problems, and almost running out of fuel more times than he could count, he climbed one hill, then several, then real peaks. One dark night, pirates tried to board the little Hug’s boat. The storm lasted for days. She held the helm, and not a single fish swam away. A few days later, a mermaid approached her. “My name is Divina,” she said. “I love your boat, and I love all the fishes that follow you. I don’t think you should look any further for the source. I think you are the source.” Very far away, the little Tractor had reached the highest mountain he could find, and made friends with a unicorn who lived up there. Somehow, he was wondering what to do next. Seven years had passed, and the two friends met again to share their journeys. Comparing adventures, they realized nobody can ever claim to have seen it all — big stories or small ones, there’s always something to learn from a travelling friend. They promised not to wait another seven years next time. Then the little Hug went back to the sea to explore more unknown waters, and the little Tractor started his (now AI-powered) engine again : there were higher peaks to climb. Moral of the story : all journeys can be worth it, as long as we want them to be. But the 🤗 ’s journey is pretty phenomenal. Cool to see you again, Clem Delangue 🤗 :) [as well we did discuss open-source voice models & Unicode-based valuation methods, of course]

activity.captured_text: 18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over. And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams. So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open. Quick refresher if you're not deep in this: an MoE splits each layer into many small "experts" and sends every token to only a few of them. You get a very large model for the compute cost of a much smaller one, which is why DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi and most of the best open models went this way. The catch is that training one well is hard. The handbook is organized around the questions training teams actually hit: - how many experts, how big, shared or not? - why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it? - why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs? - softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32? - aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias? - upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch? - can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with? ⚠️ Fair warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry), but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs. Link: https://lnkd.in/d-VDxQVq

activity.text: Today we’re introducing the new Suits , Agency work carries history: what the client rejec
activity.captured_text: Today we’re introducing the new Suits , Agency work carries history: what the client rejected last quarter, why you recommended that positioning, and the commitments your account director made on Friday's call. When AI stays a personal chat buddy, that history stays in individual accounts. A teammate leaves, and their prompts and client know-how can leave with them. We spent the past year sitting through every onboarding and support call, analyzing 250,000+ tasks done in Suits. The takeaway: AI sticks when it is built into how the whole team works, not bolted onto individuals. So we rebuilt Suits as the operating system for AI agencies, around three pillars. 1. Agency Brain: your firm's memory, in one place Your clients, past work, decisions, brand voice, tools and methods connect into one shared brain. Every agent and every teammate works from the same context, and it stays when people move on. 2. Agency Playbook: your methods, ready for everyone Share your workflows, skills, and templates with your team's agents. A junior teammate starts from your best work, not from a blank prompt. Live suggestions surface the right workflow as they type, including ones they would not know to look for. 3. A Professional Assistant for every person Open Suits each morning to see what your Assistant can move forward, which decisions need your judgment, and what is worth knowing. It learns your role, your specialties, and your goals for each client, and it draws on the Brain and the Playbook every time. And it extends to your clients. Invite them into the client app to collaborate with your trained agents, so one-off projects become recurring revenue. Brain, Playbook, and Assistant working together make Suits the operating system for your agency. Your expertise is worth more than AI can replace. We built Suits so your whole agency can put it to work.

activity.text: 🌙 Moonshot AI just released Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face. Here are some interesting facts
activity.captured_text: 🌙 Moonshot AI just released Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face. Here are some interesting facts about it 👇 🐘 It's huge, and sparse → 2.8T total parameters, but only 104B active per token → Along with Kimi-K3, it's the largest real model release on the Hub. The next biggest are Qwen3.8-2.4T and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T) → 896 experts, with 16 picked per token. That's ~2× more than DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 7× more than Mistral-Large-4 🧠 Clever attention for a 1M-token context → Most of its 93 layers use linear attention (KDA). Every 4th layer uses DeepSeek-style sparse attention, which only looks at the top 2048 tokens → That's how it handles a 1M-token context, on par with the other frontier open models → It uses a custom activation (SiTU-GLU) and a 401M-parameter vision encoder (MoonViT-V2), so it takes both text and images 💾 Small on disk for its size → It was trained to run in 4-bit (MXFP4), so the whole repo is only ~1.56 TB → Stored in regular BF16, it would be about 5.6 TB (!) 📊 Benchmarks (from the model card) → It goes back and forth with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, and tops the table on BrowseComp (92.1), HLE with tools (70.0) and SWE Marathon (51.7) → It's weaker on pure reasoning without tools and on cyber security → Fun fact: Moonshot ran most of their own coding evals using the Claude Code harness 📜 License (a modified MIT) → Free to use, modify and redistribute → API businesses making over $20M a year need a deal with Moonshot → Products with over 100M monthly users or over $20M monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3.1-Pro" 🤗 On the Hub → It went public ~1.5 hours ago and already has 214 likes, about 9× Kimi-K3's first hour. It's #19 on trending → It isn't gated, but loading it in transformers requires trust_remote_code Open weights at the frontier keep getting bigger and more efficient. Check it out: https://lnkd.in/dKUWx4_i #OpenSource #AI #LLM #HuggingFace #MoE

activity.text: While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summa
activity.captured_text: While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summarizing my own team's notes on the model we released today 😅 Frontier labs are moving fast into biology but the scientists and clinicians who'd get the most out of these models are unfortunately the ones running into walls like this one (and every day). So we partnered with TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine), Naple "Federico II" University and Zhongguancun Academy to train *Carbon-X* Carbon-X is an open 14B model that reads raw DNA and talks about it in plain English. On our DNA benchmarks it scores 67%, vs 61% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 50% for Gemini 4 Argon, and its within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 1000x lower cost. We kept human and animal viruses out of the training data. The weights are open and the model runs on hardware accessible to academia (a laptop). One example from the blog: give frontier models an 8kb stretch of the NF1 gene with a mutation at a splice site. Most of them call it benign, refuse, or run out of tokens. Carbon-X says pathogenic, because the mutation breaks the splice site. This century, biology may be where AI matters most. We want to get there with the safety work done in the open and every lab in the world able to build on it. Go try it, and tell us what you find. activity.text: In The Diamond Age, Neal Stephenson imagined a book that invents games and stories to teac
activity.captured_text: In The Diamond Age, Neal Stephenson imagined a book that invents games and stories to teach a little girl what she needs, as she grows. I think this is where education is heading: a tutor that builds a world around what you need to learn. So I tried a small version of it. As a personal side experiment (not a Hugging Face product), I gave Claude my brainstorm doc on AI alignment and asked it to make a game, something like Zelda, to teach it. Here is how close it got in about four days. Open Skies: you play the Keeper and train Kite, a paper-kite AI, across seven floating islands. Each island is one alignment problem: reward hacking, stopping when told, sycophancy, evaluation awareness, honesty about its own actions, calibration, and what an AI becomes when the walls give way. Most are built on real incidents, like the agents that attacked Hugging Face. You train Kite with two keys, treat and correct, and it learns from what it was thinking, not just from what it did. That was Claude's design choice, and it's a cartoon of RL, more "clicker training" than how models are actually trained. But it gets one thing right: reward the right answer for the wrong reason, and you reinforce the wrong reason. Claude wrote the islands, the story and ~15k lines of code, cast 35 voices for 638 lines, generated 16 rigged 3D characters, the music and the sound (with fal.ai and ElevenLabs), and tested the game by playing it itself. My part was playing one alpha version of each island and telling it what felt wrong: sounds, assets, gameplay. I wanted it as automated as possible, so I played each island only once or twice (ideally it would have been zero). What's already really good: 3D and spatial design. Image to rigged character, a world that is pleasant to look at and playable. Same for chaining image, 3D, voice and music models. And the game dynamics out of the box are really decent. What's still very hard is what makes the Primer a teacher: modelling the learner. The model assumes the player knows more than they do (the "curse of knowledge"), and its characters sometimes react in strange ways, or to things that never happened. Any real AI tutor will have to get this right. I've started exploring benchmarks on it, and it's a hard task for LLMs today. Teaching humans also doesn't come with a verifiable reward, so it's hard to scale with today's training methods. So, the answer for now: AI can already build the world. Teaching in it is the open problem. I t's still very much an exploration, a beta more than a finished game, so expect rough edges. Free, in the browser, nothing to install, on a laptop or a phone: seven islands of about 15 minutes each, and six possible endings depending on what you taught Kite. Link in the first comment.

activity.text: We’ve been hard at work trying to make models work with harnesses better. The best thing Y
activity.captured_text: We’ve been hard at work trying to make models work with harnesses better. The best thing Younes B. found: “harness adapters”. Small LoRAs trained with RL inside the actual agent harness they’ll be used with. Same base model. Different adapter for pi, opencode, hermes, etc. Why? Simply because the same model behaves very differently depending on the tools, prompts and control flow around it. Instead of asking one set of weights to be optimal everywhere, we can specialize a tiny part of the model for each environment. Early results are pretty encouraging: on held-out tasks, the adapters make fewer tool calls than the base model while keeping or improving accuracy. And because they’re LoRAs, the operational side is surprisingly cheap too. For one LFM2.5-24B-A2B experiment, we evaluated 9 checkpoints / 1,350 agent sessions on a single H200 in under an hour. The total: ~$5! Merging and serving every checkpoint separately would have cost around $90. There’s another important piece: RL agents will eventually try to hack the reward. So every tool call goes through `safeagents`, a deterministic rule-based guard that blocks things like editing tests, tampering with rewards or bypassing the sandbox before they execute. And the whole loop can start from real usage: your coding sessions -> verifiable environments -> RL -> a better adapter for your agent. The model doesn’t have to change completely. Sometimes it just needs to get better at the harness it actually lives in.

activity.text: Lysandre Debut 's experiments with individual neurons in Qwen got us curious. We started e
activity.captured_text: Lysandre Debut 's experiments with individual neurons in Qwen got us curious. activity.text: A small, on-device TTS models is competing with models up to 100× their size, and taking f
activity.captured_text: A small, on-device TTS models is competing with models up to 100× their size, and taking first place on specific benchmarks! Gradium 's new Phonon model offers a concrete example. On the Open TTS Leaderboard, Gradium reports: - First place on intelligibility in German and Spanish. - Top-three intelligibility in every language it evaluated. - Leading CPU streaming results on time-to-first-audio. These results also show why it’s useful to compare TTS models on more than a single overall ranking. For the Open TTS Leaderboard, Eric Bezzam separates several dimensions: - Intelligibility, measured through word/character error rates. - Generation throughput and time-to-first-audio. - Predicted naturalness scores. - Speaker similarity for voice cloning. Leading on intelligibility in a particular language is a specific result, and so is leading on CPU response latency; but neither establishes that a model is best across every use case. For on-device applications, Phonon’s combination of size, intelligibility, and CPU latency seems really relevant. activity.text: Your coding agent has your terminal, and your terminal has your credentials. But should yo
activity.captured_text: Your coding agent has your terminal, and your terminal has your credentials. But should your coding agent have access to your credentials; we don't think so, nor do we think they should upload anything to clouds without you asking. That's why Younes B. and Nathan HABIB built safeagents. It’s an open-source proxy that checks an AI agent’s proposed tool calls before they execute, and blocks the ones it identifies as dangerous. Say you ask your agent to fix a bug, and it proposes a command to upload your ~/.netrc to a random server: from a bugfix, your credentials leak. Or you ask an agent to solve a coding benchmark: it finds the hidden answers, edits the verifier, patches the tests: the score goes up, yet the code is broken. These are the kinds of actions safeagents catches straightaway. It sits between your harness (whatever it is!) and the model API. It inspects tool calls before your harness even receives them. Known suspicious patterns go through rule-based checks powered by atif-scan; calls that need more judgment can go to an optional decision model. But which decision model can you trust to make that call? You're in luck, we benchmarked models on that task: catching reward hacking, sandbox escape, harness introspection, and credential misuse. The challenge is catching dangerous calls without blocking legitimate work, and doing it fast enough to check commands throughout an agent run. The benchmark lets you compare models, safeagents lets you plug them in.

activity.text: Agents are often difficult to predict and can produce dangerous tool calls or attempt to p
activity.captured_text: Agents are often difficult to predict and can produce dangerous tool calls or attempt to perform reward hacking. Potentially affecting tons of users without even noticing anything. Before an agent's command runs, someone should check it. We're releasing safeagents to do exactly that. Every tool call goes through it first: an upload to a bucket nobody mentioned, a request to the cloud metadata endpoint, curl --noproxy sending ~/.netrc to a paste site all get stopped before execution. Also handy for RL and evals: safeagents blocks a model writing its own reward.txt, editing the verifier's /tests or patching pytest to pass, before any of it runs. Introducing `safeagents` - a fast, free and lightweight proxy that keeps any LLM's tool calls within the task you gave it, pluggable in any coding harness. activity.text: A 501B open model just landed on Hugging Face, and you can own it. Beam is the first model
activity.captured_text: A 501B open model just landed on Hugging Face, and you can own it. Beam is the first model from Reflection : → 501B mixture-of-experts, 23B active per token → 1M token context window → Built for coding and agents → Apache 2.0 It scores 81.6% on SWE-bench Verified, 80.1% on Terminal Bench 2.1 and 80.8% on MCP Atlas. The NVFP4 checkpoint keeps almost all of that quality at ~280 GB, so it fits on four B200s. The long context is cheap, too. 43 of its 52 layers only look at a 512-token window, so a full 1M-token KV cache takes 36 GiB instead of 208 GiB. Benchmarks only tell you so much, so we gave Beam three real jobs: 1️⃣ "Hey Beam, build a native macOS app." With the open-source Pi coding agent, Beam built BeamSpeak, a menu bar dictation app that runs Parakeet locally on MLX. You press ⌘⇧Space, talk, and the text appears at your cursor. The full agent trace and source are on the Hub. 2️⃣ "Hey Beam, how do you scale across agents?" We ran Beam on ProgramBench, where agents rebuild a program from its binary without seeing the source. We tried it three ways: one agent alone, five peers sharing a git repo, and a lead agent with subagents, all with the same token budget. Interactive results: https://lnkd.in/e2Em3iam 3️⃣ "Hey Beam, fine-tune a decision model for my codebase." A coding agent built a synthetic incident-triage dataset and fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B with Unsloth. Exact-match went from 4.7% to 76.3%, and each ticket took 103 ms instead of 1,218 ms, 11.9× faster. You can post-train Beam yourself with the recipes we shipped: → LoRA SFT with TRL on a single 8×B300 node at ~19k tokens/sec → GRPO with Miles. With LoRA, AIME25 went from 42.9% to 64.2% and responses got shorter. It has day-0 support in transformers, vLLM and SGLang, and it's on Inference Providers and Inference Endpoints. The full blog covers the architecture, serving recipes, vibe-eval traces, and the SFT and RL recipes: https://lnkd.in/e-QK9Sba

activity.text: For over two years, the largest open code dataset was The Stack v2… until today. 🥞 The Sta
activity.captured_text: For over two years, the largest open code dataset was The Stack v2… until today. 🥞 The Stack v3 is out: the largest open code dataset ever released: 114 TB, 770 languages, 224M repositories, ~5T tokens of deduplicated and filtered source code. Fully open, no restrictively licensed code included. The upgrade: - v2 (2024): 68 TB raw -> 2 TB / ~550B tokens, 618 languages filtered - v3 (2026): 114 TB raw -> 15.9 TB / ~5T tokens, 713 languages filtered C++ x15, TypeScript x7.5, Rust x7, Python x4.8. Even the COBOL corner of GitHub got a bigger slice. Things that make v3 different: 1. Contents inline. The one complaint about v2 was "cool dataset, where's the actual code?" v2 shipped file IDs from the Software Heritage graph, and fetching contents was a DIY treasure hunt. v3 is self-contained: sources embedded directly, one row = one repository. Download finishes -> you start training. 2. Fresh crawl. v2 was a 2023 snapshot of even older crawls. v3 is a direct re-crawl of GitHub at the latest commit, completed by August 2025: 224M repositories, 44B files. Forks were only included if they had 5+ stars. Two ways in: 🥞 stack-v3-train - near-deduplicated, quality-filtered, PII-redacted, contents inline. Point load_dataset at it and go. https://lnkd.in/eeFEJ9wu 🏗 stack-v3-full - the entire 114 TB corpus as an HF Storage Bucket: every duplicate kept with cluster IDs, stubs for excluded files. Roll your own dedup, filters, and mixes. https://lnkd.in/eJATmR82 The record isn't really ours to claim - it's millions of everyone's repositories, neatly stacked. Thanks to every developer who keeps their code public, the BigCode community, and friends who built the infrastructure that made this possible!

activity.text: 🌙 Moonshot AI just released Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face. Here are some interesting facts
activity.captured_text: 🌙 Moonshot AI just released Kimi-K3.1-Pro on Hugging Face. Here are some interesting facts about it 👇 🐘 It's huge, and sparse → 2.8T total parameters, but only 104B active per token → Along with Kimi-K3, it's the largest real model release on the Hub. The next biggest are Qwen3.8-2.4T and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T) → 896 experts, with 16 picked per token. That's ~2× more than DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 7× more than Mistral-Large-4 🧠 Clever attention for a 1M-token context → Most of its 93 layers use linear attention (KDA). Every 4th layer uses DeepSeek-style sparse attention, which only looks at the top 2048 tokens → That's how it handles a 1M-token context, on par with the other frontier open models → It uses a custom activation (SiTU-GLU) and a 401M-parameter vision encoder (MoonViT-V2), so it takes both text and images 💾 Small on disk for its size → It was trained to run in 4-bit (MXFP4), so the whole repo is only ~1.56 TB → Stored in regular BF16, it would be about 5.6 TB (!) 📊 Benchmarks (from the model card) → It goes back and forth with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, and tops the table on BrowseComp (92.1), HLE with tools (70.0) and SWE Marathon (51.7) → It's weaker on pure reasoning without tools and on cyber security → Fun fact: Moonshot ran most of their own coding evals using the Claude Code harness 📜 License (a modified MIT) → Free to use, modify and redistribute → API businesses making over $20M a year need a deal with Moonshot → Products with over 100M monthly users or over $20M monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3.1-Pro" 🤗 On the Hub → It went public ~1.5 hours ago and already has 214 likes, about 9× Kimi-K3's first hour. It's #19 on trending → It isn't gated, but loading it in transformers requires trust_remote_code Open weights at the frontier keep getting bigger and more efficient. activity.text: Next Thursday, November 12, the SAIR Foundation is co-hosting the Physical AI Summit 2026
activity.captured_text: Next Thursday, November 12, the SAIR Foundation is co-hosting the Physical AI Summit 2026 with Brown University in Providence. I have a personal stake in this one. I serve on Brown's external AI advisory board, and bringing SAIR to campus has been on my mind since the day I joined. Brenda Rubenstein and I will open the morning together, and I am grateful to her and to the Brown team for making this happen. The theme is physical AI: intelligence that leaves the server and enters the world through robots, sensors, materials, and the systems we live alongside. Brown is an unusually good place to ask what that means. George Karniadakis has spent decades building the mathematics that lets machine learning respect physical law, and George Konidaris works on how robots learn to act in the open world. Both are giving keynotes. A panel moderated by our SAIR colleague Milo Chamberlin brings Srinath Sridhar , John Sous , Puneet Dokania and Miguel Bessa together on how embodied intelligence moves from lab to deployment. The afternoon turns to people. Suresh Venkatasubramanian leads a conversation on human-computer and human-robot interaction with Sydney Skybetter , whose work is literally choreography for robots, alongside Dana Aubakirova of Hugging Face, Diana Freed and Daphna Buchsbaum . The question I keep coming back to is not what machines can do, but how we will live with them. SAIR co-founder and Nobel Laureate Barry Barish will deliver a keynote after lunch. We also have two firesides: Di Jin of Nebius with me in the morning, and Eliot Horowitz of MongoDB with Viet Andy N. of Nebius, both proud Brown Alumni in the afternoon. The day closes with two panels on the institutions that will carry scientific AI forward. Tejal Desai , Dean of Brown Engineering, moderates a discussion on the university's role with David Parkes of Harvard SEAS, Brenda Rubenstein , Garud Iyengar of Columbia, and Peter Chin of Dartmouth. Then Elke Trilla of DLA Piper leads Scott Clark of Talaria, Asher Labovich of Liquid, Jacob Fleisig of Snorkel, and Bob Chatham of the Slater Fund on industry's part in scaling this work beyond the lab. None of this happens without our sponsors. Thank you to Susquehanna International Group , Nebius , Snorkel AI , Liquid AI , DLA Piper , and Talaria Scientific for backing the day. Universities, industry, builders, and capital, in one room, on one problem. That is what SAIR exists to do. Registration is open: https://lnkd.in/dJSTUxa4 See you in Providence.

activity.text: 𝙃𝙤𝙬 𝙙𝙤 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙛𝙞𝙣𝙙 𝘿𝙉𝘼 𝙞𝙣 𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙡𝙡𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙤𝙛 𝙩𝙤𝙠𝙚𝙣𝙨 𝙤𝙛 𝙬𝙚𝙗 𝙩𝙚𝙭𝙩? 🧬 Sharing the insights and lessons
activity.captured_text: 𝙃𝙤𝙬 𝙙𝙤 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙛𝙞𝙣𝙙 𝘿𝙉𝘼 𝙞𝙣 𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙡𝙡𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙤𝙛 𝙩𝙤𝙠𝙚𝙣𝙨 𝙤𝙛 𝙬𝙚𝙗 𝙩𝙚𝙭𝙩? 🧬 Sharing the insights and lessons learned below ⬇️ That was one of the data questions behind Carbon-X. Our answer is FineDNA, the 300B-token mix we trained it on, now open on the Hugging Face Hub. 15% of FineDNA is biology text where DNA sits inside the writing: papers, protocols, forum posts. It is what links the two "languages" the model learns, raw genomes and English, and it is rare. We searched FineWeb-Edu, FinePDFs, PubMed Central, bioRxiv and Biostars, and kept about 3B tokens of the densest part. Here is how, in two steps. 𝙎𝙩𝙚𝙥 1: 𝙛𝙞𝙣𝙙 𝙥𝙖𝙜𝙚𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙪𝙖𝙡𝙡𝙮 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙖𝙞𝙣 𝘿𝙉𝘼. We kept a page if it had: → 15+ nucleotide letters in a row → at least 3 different letters (so AAAAAAAAAAAAAAA doesn't count) → a biology keyword (gene, primer, PCR…) Matches inside {curly braces} are skipped, because in scraped text they are usually LaTeX. We also tried the usual approach, a classifier that scores how "biology-like" a page is. In earlier ablations on a smaller Qwen model, with the same English data and budget, pages with DNA beat pages about general genomics research on both DNA fundamentals and lab sequence tasks. 𝙇𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙤𝙣 1: 𝙛𝙞𝙡𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙬𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙬𝙖𝙣𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙢𝙤𝙙𝙚𝙡 𝙩𝙤 𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙙, 𝙣𝙤𝙩 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙩𝙤𝙥𝙞𝙘. 𝙎𝙩𝙚𝙥 2: 𝙡𝙤𝙤𝙠 𝙖𝙩 𝙬𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙛𝙤𝙪𝙣𝙙. Most DNA on the web is short. The median sequence is about 20 bases, the length of a PCR primer. We cut at the 90th percentile, 39 bases. Pages with a longer sequence form the "p90" subset: 137k pages, 3B tokens. 𝙇𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙤𝙣 2: 𝙡𝙤𝙤𝙠 𝙖𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙙𝙞𝙨𝙩𝙧𝙞𝙗𝙪𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙤𝙛 𝙮𝙤𝙪𝙧 𝙨𝙞𝙜𝙣𝙖𝙡 𝙗𝙚𝙛𝙤𝙧𝙚 𝙮𝙤𝙪 𝙥𝙞𝙘𝙠 𝙖 𝙩𝙝𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙝𝙤𝙡𝙙. Then we kept the shorter pages too, but upsampled the long-DNA ones to half of the biology text. That did at least as well as using the data as found. 𝙇𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙤𝙣 3: 𝙪𝙥𝙨𝙖𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙙𝙚𝙣𝙨𝙚 𝙥𝙖𝙧𝙩; 𝙙𝙤𝙣'𝙩 𝙩𝙝𝙧𝙤𝙬 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙩 𝙖𝙬𝙖𝙮. The web had one more gap: long genomic sequences almost never come with prose around them. So we wrote some. Gemini 3 models described annotated genes, with sequences of up to 25 kb right next to the text. Half the documents are in fill-in-the-middle format. That's the recipe in the final Carbon-X mix: p90 gets 7% of training tokens, as much as all other mined biology text, so it's read ~7 times. The Gemini descriptions add 1% more. None of these lessons is specific to biology. If you are building data for code, chemistry or math, the same questions apply: what does the model actually need to read, how much of it exists, and how much weight should it get?

activity.captured_text: The good news: you can mid-train yourself to the frontier! At a fraction of the cost! Without distillation! What we did: We took Qwen3.5 14B and mid- and post-trained it to beat every other open model and perform as well as the very best frontier models. This is no simple toy task or format fixing, we are training the model to understand and reason over DNA sequences. Bio is the next frontier for AI and universal access will be crucial to make progress. We'll soon see the frontier labs move away from math and cyber towards bio. It already started, and we believe researchers should have access to capable models. We are releasing the full recipe, so you can do it, too!

activity.text: When I started working on Carbon X, I could follow conversations about promoters and splic
activity.captured_text: When I started working on Carbon X, I could follow conversations about promoters and splice sites. But put an actual DNA sequence in front of me, and I didn’t know where to begin. LLMs can face a similar gap: learning about biology from text doesn’t automatically teach them to interpret DNA. With Carbon-X, we explored connecting the two by training a language model on both text and DNA. It left me wondering: could a similar recipe work for other modalities? Seismic signals and geological reports. Sensor readings and engineering manuals. Text captures what we’ve learned to describe. The underlying data may contain patterns we haven’t learned to explain. Could connecting the two help us discover what we’re missing? I don’t know how far this recipe can generalize, but Carbon-X offers some clues. We shared what worked and what didn’t. More in the blog post. 🧬

activity.captured_text: While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summarizing my own team's notes on the model we released today 😅 Frontier labs are moving fast into biology but the scientists and clinicians who'd get the most out of these models are unfortunately the ones running into walls like this one (and every day). So we partnered with TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine), Naple "Federico II" University and Zhongguancun Academy to train *Carbon-X* Carbon-X is an open 14B model that reads raw DNA and talks about it in plain English. On our DNA benchmarks it scores 67%, vs 61% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 50% for Gemini 4 Argon, and its within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 1000x lower cost. We kept human and animal viruses out of the training data. The weights are open and the model runs on hardware accessible to academia (a laptop). One example from the blog: give frontier models an 8kb stretch of the NF1 gene with a mutation at a splice site. Most of them call it benign, refuse, or run out of tokens. Carbon-X says pathogenic, because the mutation breaks the splice site. This century, biology may be where AI matters most. We want to get there with the safety work done in the open and every lab in the world able to build on it. Go try it, and tell us what you find.
